MurimJak rated it
Other reviews by this user
October 21, 2025
Status: --
The novel "Sword Devouring Swordmater" starts out clichéd: a protagonist who simply wants a normal life but is forced to grow strong in a world ruled by might. He rises from a "nobody" to a great warrior, driven by a mysterious and forbidden lineage.

The biggest appeal of the work is the main character (MC) : he is not a perfect machine. The MC fails, complains about the pain of getting stronger, and is not ashamed to "crawl" to advance, making him more human than typical clichéd heroes.

The power scale, based... more>> on "great kingdoms" and subdivisions, is intriguing but a bit confusing initially, only becoming clearer from the third great kingdom onwards.

In short, the novel compensates for its predictable start with a realistic protagonist and an engaging progression. <<less

Vanzallius rated it
Other reviews by this user
December 30, 2025
Status: c124
Make no mistake, this novel absolutely has great moments. The author really knows what makes a good underdog story, writing scenes that really put one at the edge of their seat as the MC overcomes impossible odds. There is a simple underlying story of a nobody rising to the top to take revenge on the world.

However, while this is all well and good, there is a reason why my rating dropped off sharply when I'd reached the triple digits. This novel suffers from a problem many other WN's of this... more>> genre do: Poor world building. Simply put, just like with Regressed Mecenary, this author has no idea how to write believable logistics pertaining to kingdom building and warfare, as well as how to fit them all on a timeline that any reader can follow. We're lead to believe that armies can simply be plopped down and moved around at the drop of a head as if we're in a game of Civilization, or that domains can be built and populated by throwing money at them as if we're attracting park-goers in RollerCoaster Tycoon.

That's just not how the world works. There are many fantasy elements that could potentially affect how all of this functions, but at no point does the author do a decent job at incorporating them and/or explaining how. Now, in a lot of fantasy novels you can simply choose to omit the complex parts and that's fine, but you can't avoid it if a lot of the plot starts depending on them - and this is exactly where we're at the 100 chapter mark. It absolutely kills the readers' suspension of disbelief if you engage in all these topics and make them critical to the plot without a solid plan.

And another symptom of this is the absolutely incomprehensible timeline. Similarly to Regressed Mercenary, you watch it go from scene A to scene B within a single chapter, and suddenly an unspecified amount of time passed. Trying to piece things together contextually, suddenly it seems as if one part of the world was suspended in time, while another has moved forward by weeks, or even months? I was being abstract for the sake of avoiding spoilers, but I'll briefly give a concrete example.

Spoiler

MC is sitting in his domain, having had war declared on him. Suddenly, within a matter of days, an entire army is sitting at his doorstep, supposedly big enough to take on a nation. MC demands noble kid from their domain to come all the way over. They do. Ten days later, a duel take place after which noble kid gets in trouble. Big Swordmaster dad also starts making his way over. Somehow, in parallel, the prince not only took over the crown by killing his father, he even had the Swordmaster leaving his domain all planned out, and somehow not only scrambles together his army, but even takes over all of the cities of the Swordmaster's house, somehow all while MC, swordmaster dad, and his kids are left watching this. How in the mother of f*ck does any of this work? Well, we're never told.

[collapse]

For people wanting to read this, ask yourself: Do you care about world building and are you trying to see the world from the character's perspective when you read? If the answer is yes, you might lose enjoyment as soon as the world starts opening up. If not, you definitely have a decent story with swords and cool powers. <<less

Dreyerboys rated it
Other reviews by this user
February 2, 2026
Status: c140
I feel conflicted about this novel. Like other people have said, it has some pretty high high's, but some low low's.

The good:

The author does a good job of providing motivation. We get to see a lot of the characters' backstories, their reason for their emotions and behaviors, and what they want to be. This is often also portrayed in each character's fighting style/sword style. The progression of their power is often a representation of their past, which I quite like.

The plot is quite simple, but I don't think that's necessarily... more>> a bad thing. It's a revenge story. As in, the whole novel is about revenge. He doesn't finish his revenge in 10 chapters, then goes to an academy to fart around, then decides to get stronger for whatever reason. There's a clear target for revenge. There's a clear strength-level target. There's a clear progression. Whether that's good or bad is up to you, but compared to other slop, I think this is fine.

As for the characters and their dialogue, I'd say that, for the most part, it feels somewhat real. The only person who feels out of place is the Master, but I'll get to him later.

The fights are decent enough. I don't think I'd call them exceptional, but they're not bad. I have good and bad things to say about them, so I'll just say that the way the fights are described is good.

The bad:

The Master. To me, this guy's presence is WAY too significant. He's pivotal in just about every scene. He's always there. He always knows exactly what the MC should do and will always let him know. Dude talks more than the actual MC. Not to mention, whenever people know about/can see the Master, they really only care about him. Maybe the Orc Shaman is the only one who likes the MC, but that's only because of his bloodline. I hate this character. The only good thing about him is that he significantly shortens the amount of time the MC needs to get stronger, because, well, he knows everything. He's just a Deus Ex Machina sitting on the MCs shoulders.

The MC himself isn't bad per se, but his personality traits feel a bit forced. I don't really know how to describe it, he just feels artificial (yeah, I know he's a fictional character, but even then...). I'll give an example. When the MC meets his Master, the Master says that the MC has a very sensitive and suspicious nature. He says he's curious and doubtful of everything. From then on, the MC is curious and doubtful of everything. Whereas, before that moment, the only scene of him being "doubtful" is him looking at a painting of his ancestor and doubting their bloodline's glorious past. That too, when both him and his father are untalented and weak. Not anywhere close to swordmasters.

Onto the plot. Now, I think the structure of the plot is fine. What I'm not the biggest fan of is that the MC literally has zero agency. His Master tells him how to get stronger and where to go to do so. His main enemy wants him to get stronger, so he's constantly sending "trials" at the MC for amusement. Basically, just too many annoying and intrusive characters. MC hasn't made his own decision since like chapter 3 when he decided to get revenge. Everything after that was decided for him.

The world-building is okay. I see some people complain about it. Some people like it. I think it's whatever. It's a bit all over the place, and some things definitely don't make sense. Sometimes timelines are weird and don't add up. I just think, for the most part, it's needless complexity, but not inherently bad.

Overall, I'd say it's pretty good. It has some glaring faults, but it's simple, brainless, yet emotionally complex enough to enjoy without much thought. The power system is straightforward, a bit unique, and well thought-out. If you don't like the mini 5-10 chapter arcs, you can honestly skip them and not miss much. At some point over the next few chapters, it'll tell you what you missed.

It's decent enough to pass the time with. <<less

Ravenpeko rated it
Other reviews by this user
March 3, 2026
Status: c123
Lemme just say this b4 I start the review, this is a novel that suffers from the usual issues appearing and becoming more and more significant as time novel goes on.

So MC is just a guy livin in a small village with his "supposed once great, fallen noble family". MC didn't believe that his family was great back in the days. One day, a Swordmaster comes and kills everyone in the village, but he spares MC because he's not eighteen yet. MC trains for naught for a whole year and... more>> the family heirloom sword talks to him. Turns out, the founder (the strongest human like ever) resides in that sword and he teaches MC of his bloodline and abilities. This is a story about revenge and perseverance.

Pros:

  • The author is really good at writing the parts when MC is lost and needs motivation. Often times, our MC will think "There's no way I can beat him." or "Is this worth all the pain?". Then the MC will remember his true goal and what he his to do in order to achieve that (usually on his master's cue). You can really feel how much despair MC is going thru and how much this revenge means to him.
  • So our MC eats swords, and by eating them, he goes thru the owner's memories and assimilates with the sword. Thru this, we get to see many different stories which are all pretty unique and meaningful.
Cons:

  • The character dynamics are assssss. The FL goes along with MC on a whim because of mc's master. The prince and the swordmaster both aren't doing sht to the MC even tho, they learned of his identity (with the s*upid reason of "ohh, he's not over eighteen yet"). One of the swordmaster of the 5 great families are also flawed and dumb af. Mc's master as well. The master always only gives MC tiny hints and stuff when he could've just told him. He only did start telling him everything when there was no time because someone very strong was coming. Though, this means he could just help MC as much as he can no matter the situation, and MC is always in a time crunch. But I digress.
  • As I said b4, this novel suffers from the triple dight curse. So much novels start doing downhill after reaching chapter 100-120. The author often lose sight of proper world building and development which leads to a big mess that processes unnaturally. Vanzallius explained what happened perfectly so go read that.
  • All the pros I mentioned gets pretty repetitive. They'll keep reusing the same motivations and sht whenever stuff happens. Like I get it, it's well written, but using the same notion 5 times diminishes the effects. Even the stories of the swords start to get a bit boring.
Overall, it starts off pretty strong, but goes downhill. Turn off your brain, ignore the world building and development issues, and read it as a manhwa with pretty pictures, then it'll be good. I'll prb finish it once all the chaps are out, but for now, it's gotten stale. <<less
